About: A Charge in a Magnetic Field — The Clock That Ignores the Speed

Source

Topic
Moving charges & magnetism (JEE / NCERT Class 12)
Concept
The period of a charged particle's circular motion in a uniform magnetic field is T = 2πm/(qB) — independent of its speed.
Serves
Circular & helical motion in B; the fact that a magnetic force does no work; the principle behind the cyclotron.
Inquiry
Double the entry speed. What happens to the time for one orbit?
Misconception
“A faster particle must go round faster.” The path lengthens in exact proportion, so the period is unchanged.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Set the scene

An electron is fired into a region of uniform magnetic field B (into the page). It enters perpendicular to B, so the magnetic force curves it into a closed circle.

The whole circle is drawn from the start and the electron runs round it. The orbit clock at the top right sweeps its hand once per orbit.

2 · Predict — the star question

You are about to double the entry speed v, holding B and the entry angle fixed. What happens to the time for one complete orbit?

3 · Observe

Drag the entry speed slider up and down. Watch the circle swell and shrink while the orbit clock keeps exactly the same beat.

Read the two numbers below — radius r changes, period T does not budge.

4 · Tilt the entry

Now the electron is given a component along B: the entry angle tilts from 90° to 45°. The perpendicular component still winds a circle at the same beat; the parallel component is untouched by the magnetic force and drifts straight along B.

The result is a helix, advancing one pitch per turn. The clock still marks the same beat.

5 · Resolve

The period T = 2πm/(qB) depends on the particle and the field — never on how fast it is going. That independence is what makes a cyclotron possible: a fixed-frequency accelerator can kick the particle at the same rhythm no matter what energy it has reached.

And note: |v| and KE never change. A magnetic force is always perpendicular to the motion, so it does no work at all.

The Physics

Charge in a Magnetic Field — The Clock That Ignores the Speed · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

An electron is fired into a region of uniform magnetic field, and the sim draws its path, an orbit clock and two live numbers, the radius r and the period T. You set the entry speed v and the field strength B. This motion is the working principle of the cyclotron and the mass spectrometer.

What you'll learn

  • What a magnetic force does to the motion of a charged particle, and what it cannot do.
  • How the size of the path and the time for one lap depend on v and B.
  • What changes when the electron enters at a slant to the field.
An electron enters a uniform field. The blue ⊗ marks show B pointing into the page.

What's on screen

  • The electron and its path, drawn over a grid of faint ⊗ marks that stand for the field B into the page.
  • Velocity arrow, labelled speed v, always along the direction of motion.
  • Orbit clock (top right): its hand sweeps once round for every lap, and a counter below it tallies the laps.
  • Live readouts: the radius r and the period T, in mm and ns.

03

A magnetic force turns the electron but never speeds it up

The magnetic force on a moving charge is

F⃗ = q v⃗ × B⃗
F⃗ is perpendicular to both v⃗ and B⃗.

Because F⃗ is always at right angles to the motion, it does no work on the charge. It changes the direction of v⃗ but not its size, so the speed and the kinetic energy stay fixed. For an electron entering at right angles to B into the page, the force points toward one side only, so the path bends into a circle. Seen on screen, the electron runs clockwise, because its charge is negative.

See itRun the electron at v = 1.00 × 10⁶ m/s in B = 10 mT. Watch for: the arrow labelled speed v turning round the circle at a constant length, always at right angles to the dashed radius line.
04

The radius grows in proportion to the speed

On a circle the magnetic force must supply the centripetal force: m v² / r = |q| v B. Cancel one v and solve for r:

r = m v / (|q| B)
Twice the speed, twice the radius. Twice the field, half the radius.

A faster electron is harder to turn, so it swings wider. For the electron at v = 1.00 × 10⁶ m/s in B = 10 mT the sim reads r = 0.569 mm. Doubling v to 2.00 × 10⁶ m/s gives r = 1.137 mm. Doubling B instead, to 20 mT at the original speed, halves r to 0.284 mm.

See itSet v = 2.00 × 10⁶ m/s with B = 10 mT. Watch for: r reading 1.137 mm, twice the 0.569 mm it showed at v = 1.00.
05

The period depends on the field, not on the speed

One lap is a distance 2πr covered at speed v, so T = 2πr / v. Put in r = m v / (|q| B) and the v cancels:

T = 2π m / (|q| B)
Only the particle (m, q) and the field B appear.

A faster electron travels a longer circle, in exact proportion, so each lap takes the same time. The sim shows T = 3.572 ns at 10 mT for every speed from 0.2 to 4.0 × 10⁶ m/s, which is about 280 million laps per second. Only B moves it: T = 1.786 ns at 20 mT and 0.893 ns at 40 mT.

See itSet v = 4.00 × 10⁶ m/s with B = 10 mT. Watch for: r at 2.274 mm, four times the starting value, while T still reads 3.572 ns.
06

A slanted entry draws a helix

Split the velocity into a part v⊥ = v sin θ across B and a part v∥ = v cos θ along B, where θ is the angle between v⃗ and B⃗. The force acts on v⊥ only, so that part winds a circle of radius m v⊥ / (|q| B) at the same period T. The part along B feels no force and drifts on steadily:

pitch = v∥ T
The distance advanced along B in one turn.

At the sim's 45° entry with v = 1.00 × 10⁶ m/s and B = 10 mT, v⊥ = v∥, so r = 0.402 mm, T is still 3.572 ns, and the pitch is 2.53 mm, which equals 2π r. The speed v is still constant, because the force does no work.

See itSwitch to the sim's helix view at v = 1.00 × 10⁶ m/s and B = 10 mT. Watch for: a coil along the dashed B axis, r reading 0.402 mm, T unchanged at 3.572 ns and a pitch label of 2.53 mm.
07

Where it matters

  • Cyclotron. The particle crosses the gap between two D-shaped halves twice per lap. Since T does not depend on speed, an alternating voltage of one fixed frequency f = |q| B / (2π m) can keep boosting it as its orbit grows. This holds while v is small compared with the speed of light.
  • Mass spectrometer. Ions with the same v and charge in the same B follow circles with r proportional to m, so different masses land at different places.
  • Tracks in a detector. The radius of a curved track gives the momentum, p = |q| B r, and the direction of the bend gives the sign of the charge.
08

Summary

In one line. A magnetic force bends a moving charge into a circle without changing its speed, and v, B, q and m together fix the radius and the lap time.

Key points

  • F⃗ = q v⃗ × B⃗ is perpendicular to v⃗, so it does no work and the speed stays fixed.
  • r = m v⊥ / (|q| B) grows with speed and shrinks with field.
  • T = 2π m / (|q| B) has no v in it. A slanted entry adds a drift along B, so the path becomes a helix of pitch v∥ T.

Common mix-ups

  • "A faster particle must go round faster." It goes round a bigger circle, in exact proportion, so each lap takes the same time.
  • "The magnetic force speeds the particle up." It is perpendicular to the motion, so it only turns it. The kinetic energy cannot change.

Things to try on your own

  • Drag v from 0.2 to 4.0 at B = 10 mT and read r and T at each end.
  • Raise B until T first reads below 1 ns, and note that B. Then read r at v = 1.00.
  • Set B = 2 mT and v = 4.0 and see how far the circle runs off the view.
